So after some prodding from @Native, I've decided to share some of the things I've learned and thought about over the past few years. I'll try to do one a week, probably on Sunday, schedule permitting. This week's topic was chosen based on its potential to branch off into many other fields, depending on what people want to talk about. I already have the topic for next week planned out, because I don't think I'll be able to fit both parts into one post.

Today's topic is a pair of related questions: can thoughts think? Do ideas have identity?

Strange questions, I know, but I'm not talking about simple thoughts like "what's for dinner?" or "should I wear a jacket?". I want to focus on much larger thoughts that take multiple people and a good chunk of time to fully realize. Those ideas that take on a life of their own. They grow, adapt, reproduce, and so forth. Just like us. Just like every form of life. Does that mean that they are actually alive, or do they just appear alive? They can't exist on their own, after all. Thoughts need thinkers.

But then, we don't really exist on our own, do we? At least, not for very long. We need food, water, air, the right temperature, a place to live. A vacuum is a magical place that turns people into corpses. Perhaps our minds are just the meadows that ideas frolic in. Whether that's metaphorically true or literally true I'll save for another time. You may also notice some similarities with Plato's world of ideals, but that is not actually what got me started on this. Perhaps a few examples will help.

What do you know about Batman? Probably a good deal. I think the average person could tell me his name, the city he lives in, what happened to his parents, as well as give a brief description of his personality and moral code. Can you give the same level of information about your friends and family? I know for a fact that Batman would never kill a criminal, but I'm not so sure what my mother would do in the same situation. That's odd, isn't it? Not because we don't take the time to really know other people, but because other people are individuals. Batman is a collection of portrayals of actors, writers, and artists. You couldn't even say the the first Batman is the "real" Batman, because he was based off of Zorro! And yet, despite all of those people and all of the those interpretations, the same basic foundation shines through. Why?

The second example is a short story. A woman passes by a beggar on her way to church. She doesn't give him anything on the way there, but after hearing about Jesus and his charity, she goes back and buys the beggar lunch. Did the woman help the beggar, or did Christ help the beggar through the woman? Your personal beliefs don't even need to apply here. You can believe that Jesus is with us all in spirit, and you can believe that a historical Jesus never existed. Neither belief changes the fact that the idea of Jesus exists, and was responsible for the woman's actions.

My goal with this post is to have you think about what you are thinking about. Observing your own thoughts is a form of meditation and self-control. Maybe you should reexamine the phrase "food for thought". Maybe you should consider that the road between you and your thoughts goes both way. What even are "your thoughts"? I probably wouldn't tell you even if I could. Not my job. Next week I'll address the question "If thoughts and ideas are their own separate things, then what happens when several people have the same thoughts at the same time?"
